findings.title: The egress classifier called shared address space PUBLIC and an IPv4-mapped address by its IPv6 flags, so a PUBLIC-only grant reached an inside network
findings.subsystem: the egress authority: the address classes a grant permits

files.lines: classify_address, which the decision's class check and both of the socket guard's class checks ask

findings.behavior: A grant permits address classes, PUBLIC only by default. classify_address took PUBLIC to mean whatever was not unspecified, loopback, multicast, link-local, private or reserved by the standard library's flags. The shared address space 100.64.0.0/10 is none of those and is not global, so it read as PUBLIC, though AddressClass.PRIVATE lists it: a PUBLIC-only grant authorized a request resolved to 100.64.0.1, and the socket guard, resolving a granted name itself, connected to it. An IPv4 address carried in IPv6 was classified by its IPv6 flags, and where the interpreter answers those as IPv6, as CPython 3.12.3 in this container does and 3.12.13 and 3.13.17 do not (D-2026-195), ::ffff:127.0.0.1 and ::ffff:0.0.0.0 read as PRIVATE, so a grant permitting private ranges and not loopback reached loopback, and a mapped public address read as SPECIAL. Rated P1: the scale puts a security-boundary violation at P0, and this one is held at P1 because the host the grant names still bounds what is asked for; the inside network is reached when such a name resolves there, the rebinding case the class check exists for.
findings.invariant: An address is classified as what a connection to it reaches, and a grant reaches only the classes it names.
findings.mechanism: PUBLIC was the fall-through after a list of flags rather than what is globally reachable, and the flags of an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address are the IPv6 address's, not those of the IPv4 address a connection reaches.
findings.reproduction: At 2e8e7f2, by tests/test_egress_perimeter.py: classify_address of 100.64.0.0 to 100.127.255.255 is PUBLIC; a PUBLIC-only grant authorizes a request resolved to 100.64.0.1 or 100.127.255.254; the socket guard, with the name resolving to 100.64.0.1 and its connect recorded rather than made, connects; a PRIVATE-only grant authorizes ::ffff:127.0.0.1 and ::ffff:0.0.0.0. Before the test was written, a probe in this session's container connected through the guard to 100.64.0.1:443, which is live there, and closed the connection without sending anything.
findings.observed: Found reading agent_substrate/netauth.py in full, which had been read in part.
findings.expected: 100.64.0.0/10 PRIVATE, ::ffff:a.b.c.d classified as a.b.c.d, and both refused under a grant that does not name their class.
findings.correction: classify_address classifies an IPv4-mapped address as the IPv4 address it carries, and an address that is none of the other classes and not global as PRIVATE. The decision and the guard both ask it, so both hold the corrected classes: the guard's own resolution of a granted name refuses a candidate in shared address space.
findings.residual_risk: A mapped public address, which read as SPECIAL and was refused, is PUBLIC: a connection to it reaches a public address. NAT64 and 6to4 addresses are still classified by their IPv6 flags, SPECIAL and PRIVATE here, which refuses them under a PUBLIC grant; the IPv4 address a translator would reach is not derived. 240.0.0.0/4 and the broadcast address read as PRIVATE rather than SPECIAL; neither carries a TCP connection. The classes are the standard library's, at the interpreter in use; the mapped-address rule is held on any interpreter by a test that puts the older answers back (D-2026-195). The guard tests on an IPv6 socket skip where none can be made, as in this session's container. The guard is not containment, and the module says so.

findings.title: Anyone could put an egress service contract in force, and the first contract by name among those claiming a host decided for it

files.lines: register_service and NetworkAuthority.apply on network.service; service_for
the second reader's fold of network.service, _sub_service

findings.behavior: A service contract narrows what a grant permits on the hosts it claims: the operations under contract and a per-task budget. Registering one asked nothing of its registrar, under a role registry too, and a request was decided by the first registered service, by name, among those claiming its host. An actor holding no role registered a contract for a host another principal's grant covered: on reload the granted request was refused by it, and the second reader reported nothing. And a wider contract under a name that sorts first lifted a narrower one's limits: with zz-contract permitting GET /v1/read once per task, aa-anything, permitting GET / a thousand times and registered by an actor holding no role, made GET /v1/admin allowed. Rated P1 with AUD-015, an unauthorized record taking effect on authority; the grant still bounds the host, port, method and path.
findings.invariant: A contract for a host is put in force only by an authority over egress to it, and one host is decided by one contract.
findings.mechanism: register_service and the reducer checked a contract's form, and that a service id was not registered again with other terms; they asked no role, and service_for returns the first service by id whose patterns match the host.
findings.reproduction: At 2e8e7f2, by tests/test_egress_perimeter.py: under a role registry granting EGRESS_ISSUER over api.example.org to eve alone, mallory registers a contract for it and the primary and the second reader both take it; a wider contract under an earlier name, registered beside a narrower one, decides for the host; and with no role registry two contracts claiming one host are both put in force.

findings.expected: A registration by an actor without EGRESS_ISSUER over every host it claims refused, and a second contract for a claimed host refused, by both readers.
findings.correction: A registration is refused unless its registrar holds EGRESS_ISSUER over every host it claims, at the position it is written and on replay, when a role registry is in force; and a registration claiming a host that a registered service's patterns also match is refused, with or without one, by netauth.patterns_overlap. A history holding two contracts for one host, or one registered by an actor without the role, no longer loads; none is known. With no role registry, anyone may still contract a host no contract claims, as anyone may issue an egress grant there.

findings.title: The agent directory took an escalation answer that left the question open, and the next answer replaced it

files.lines: AgentDirectory.apply on agent.escalation.answer

findings.behavior: An escalation answer moves the question to ANSWERED, or, from its asker, WITHDRAWN. The directory read an answer record's state from the payload and took any state but WITHDRAWN on the answer path: an answer whose state was OPEN recorded a person's answer and its author on a question still open, and the next answer, by another person, replaced it. answer() and withdraw() never write such a record. findings.invariant: An answer closes the question it answers, and a recorded answer is not replaced.
findings.mechanism: The reducer branched only on WITHDRAWN, and wrote the payload's state back whatever it was.
findings.reproduction: At 219f377, by tests/test_agent_directory_records.py: two registered humans and an agent's escalation; an answer record from the first human with state OPEN loads, holding that answer on an open question, and the second human's answer then loads over it, while the second reader notes the first record.
findings.observed: Found reading agent_substrate/agents.py in full, which had been read in part.
findings.expected: EscalationError on load naming the record, where the second reader notes it.
findings.correction: The directory refuses an answer record that moves the question to any state but ANSWERED or WITHDRAWN, and one naming a state that does not exist, in its own words.
findings.residual_risk: A history holding such a record no longer loads; none is known, and only a registered human principal could have written one, around the directory. Rated P2 for the readers' disagreement; the record reached nothing beyond its escalation.

findings.title: A task.evidence record by any actor at any time before the verdict was taken for a governed capture, so a report no check produced was admitted

files.lines: GovernedOrigins._view
reconstruct_tasks on task.evidence, and _execution
GovernedTasks._artifacts_of

findings.behavior: An admission asks that the verification report and the result bundle each be captured by a governed task that stood VERIFIED before the transition. A capture is a task.evidence record, which the governed runner writes, as the actor 'system', while the task executes (_capture, between EXECUTING and the outcome). Both readers of origin -- the store's GovernedOrigins._view and the independent reconstruct_tasks -- took every task.evidence record naming the task as a capture of it, from any actor, at any position before the verdict. An actor holding no role appended a task.evidence record naming a report it wrote itself to a genuine, independently executed check task, after the task completed and before its verdict; the report held every content rule of a VerificationResult, in other bytes than the check produced. Both readers counted it as captured by that VERIFIED check, and the store admitted a scientific_result citing it: a report no governed check produced authorized a result. The decision proof's _execution named the producer of a bundle the same way, from the last record naming it.
findings.invariant: What a governed task produced is what its runner captured while it ran; a record by anyone else, or at any other time, is not a capture.
findings.mechanism: Origin asked which task.evidence records named a task, never which were the runner's captures of it while it executed.
findings.reproduction: At 0278dcf, by a governed run: a model run and its independent check as governed tasks; during the check, after it completes and before its verdict, another principal appends a task.evidence record naming the check task, whose artifact is the genuine report with its agreement's resolutions divided by a thousand. g.decide(run, that report) returns VERIFIED; the store loads the result VERIFIED; the independent reader admits it. Also by tests/test_second_reader_rules.py, by hand, on a legacy history.
findings.observed: Found reading agent_substrate/reconstruct.py in full, which had been read in part, and tracing the capture back through both readers of origin.
findings.expected: The result REJECTED, and the readers to admit nothing on a report the governed check did not capture.
findings.correction: A capture is counted only from a task.evidence record written by the runner ('system', the module constant CAPTURER) while the task is EXECUTING, in GovernedOrigins._view, reconstruct_tasks, the decision proof's _execution, and GovernedTasks._artifacts_of (which answers a duplicate submission). A record by another principal, or after the run, is not applied and is reported. A check task whose history already holds such a record is refused by its own separate-process verification, so no verdict stands on it. A task executes only before its one verdict, so the checks that a capture preceded the verdict, which the rule implies, are removed from GovernedOrigins._producers, captured_by and artefacts_of and from the second reader's _sci_task_producers: the rule is the one guard, and each half of it is held by a case that breaks that half alone.
findings.residual_risk: The runner writes as 'system' on an unauthenticated log, so on such a log any writer may still use that name; the attestation of a governed history binds it, and AUD-063 makes the admission readers hold a governed history to its attestations. A capture made while the task executes is the runner's whoever it names, by construction.

findings.title: The scheduler's replay took an enqueue its writer refuses: a resource need or a citation of any kind, so one record stopped the queue or cancelled its capacity
findings.subsystem: the scheduler: replay of an enqueue

files.lines: Scheduler._reauthorize_enqueue
_sub_enqueue

findings.behavior: enqueue() refuses a resource need that is not a whole, non-negative number of a named resource, and a citation that is not a sha256 digest. _reauthorize_enqueue restates the writer's other rules on replay and not these two, so an enqueue appended directly, by its own submitter, became state. One whose need was a string, or whose citation was a number, made readiness -- documented as total -- raise TypeError, so ready_queue() and reconcile() raised for the whole queue, reconcile stopping at that job. One whose need was -5 slots cancelled other jobs' use of the capacity: at a capacity of two slots, five jobs were dispatched at once, and the in-flight count read -1. The second reader asked nothing of either, nor of an enqueue's lease end or of what a job waits on: an enqueue naming a lease end, or waiting on a job never enqueued, on a cancelled one or on more jobs than the scheduler allows, read clean there, though the primary refuses each.
findings.invariant: A record the writer refuses is refused on replay; readiness answers for every job replay admits.
findings.mechanism: The enqueue's validation of resources and citations lived on the write path alone; capacity is rightly not re-checked on replay, and the type of a need went with it.
findings.reproduction: At c82541e: an enqueue appended directly by its submitter with resources {'slots': 'many'} loads; ready_queue() and reconcile() raise TypeError. With requires_evidence [7], reconcile() raises TypeError. With resources {'slots': -5} at a capacity of 2, dispatch() hands out that job and four more; in_flight_resources() is {'slots': -1}. The writer refuses each of the three. And at c82541e, enqueues appended directly naming a lease end of 7, a dependency never enqueued, a cancelled dependency, or 65 dependencies, each refused by load(), are folded by reconstruct_subsystems with no anomaly.
findings.observed: Found reading agent_substrate/scheduler.py in full, comparing each enqueue() refusal with what _reauthorize_enqueue restates.
findings.expected: Each such record refused on replay at its position, as the writer refuses it.
findings.correction: _reauthorize_enqueue refuses a citation that is not a digest, a need that is not a whole, non-negative number of a resource named by a non-empty str, and a capability, idempotency key or task named by anything but a str. The writer's dry run refuses the same before anything is written. The second reader restates the citation and need rules in _sub_enqueue, and the enqueue's lease end and what a job waits on: a list of at most the scheduler's bound of jobs, each enqueued before it and each still able to succeed, derived from its own edge table. Capacity is still not re-checked: it is the replaying executor's.
findings.residual_risk: A refused record makes the history unloadable for the scheduler, as every record its reducer refuses does: fail closed, by the module's design, naming the record.

findings.title: No grant of possession was bounded in length, and a dispatch record named its own lease end, so the renewal bound bounded nothing

_sub_job_transition, _sub_lease_renew

findings.behavior: A lease may be renewed MAX_LEASE_RENEWALS (16) times, 'otherwise a worker holds the job forever by asking often enough, which is the same as no lease'. Neither dispatch() nor a renewal bounded the length it asked for: dispatch() with lease_seqs 10**15 and one renewal of 10**15 were both accepted. A renewal's end is computed from its position because 'a record that named its own expiry could name any'; a dispatch's end was taken from its record by both readers, and a dispatch record appended by another principal, naming itself the holder and an end of 2**62, replayed in both. reconcile() never reclaimed the job: the handover edges are refused while a lease is live, and this one did not lapse.
findings.invariant: A lease is a deadline: each grant of possession reaches a bounded distance, so the renewal count bounds how long an attempt holds its job.
findings.mechanism: The bound was put on the number of extensions and not on their length, and the end a dispatch names was read rather than judged.
findings.reproduction: At c82541e: dispatch(lease_seqs=10**15) returns a lease ending at 10**15 + 3; renew_lease(lease_seqs=10**15) extends one to 10**15 + 4; a READY -> DISPATCHED record by 'mallory' naming herself holder and lease_expires_after_seq 2**62 loads, reconcile() leaves the job DISPATCHED, and the second reader records nothing.
findings.observed: Found reading agent_substrate/scheduler.py in full, following MAX_LEASE_RENEWALS to what it bounds.
findings.expected: A grant past a stated bound refused at the writer and on replay, in both readers.
findings.correction: MAX_LEASE_SEQS (1,000,000 positions) bounds one grant: dispatch() and a renewal refuse a longer one, and replay refuses a dispatch whose lease ends farther than that past its own position -- the writer's end, at + 1 + lease_seqs, lands no farther than lease_seqs past its record. With MAX_LEASE_RENEWALS no attempt holds a job for more than 17,000,000 positions past its dispatch. The second reader restates the bound on both.

findings.title: Under a role registry no grant stands behind the task machine's SCHEDULER and SYSTEM moves, so any principal may reject, cancel or invalidate a task
findings.subsystem: the task projection: the control plane's roles

files.lines: _TASK_REGISTRY_ROLES; GovernedTasks._project on task.transition; GovernedTasks._move and invalidate
_TASK_ROLE_BEHIND

findings.behavior: Under a role registry a task move claiming SUBMITTER, WORKER or VERIFIER needs PROPOSER, EXECUTOR or VERIFIER over the tool, where it is written and on replay in both readers. A move claiming SCHEDULER or SYSTEM needs nothing: the edge alone decides it. Those two roles validate, queue, lease and requeue a task, time it out, reject or cancel it, and move a VERIFIED task to INVALIDATED. A principal holding no grant invalidated a VERIFIED task through invalidate() on the write path and by a record appended directly, rejected a CREATED task as SCHEDULER and cancelled one as SYSTEM, and both readers accepted each move. On a governed history, every record signed, a registered party no grant names signed the same invalidation, and the primary, the second reader and the separate process each accepted it. An invalidation is what GovernedModelRuns follows: a result resting on the task loses its origin, and following the invalidation makes the result STALE. The record authority binds its own SYSTEM to VERIFIER or PROMOTER over the kind, and the report's trust-boundary matrix named only the three granted task roles.
findings.invariant: Under a registry, every move a reader applies is made by a principal a grant names for it.
findings.mechanism: By stated design: _TASK_REGISTRY_ROLES and the second reader's _TASK_ROLE_BEHIND map SUBMITTER, WORKER and VERIFIER to registry roles and leave SCHEDULER and SYSTEM out, as moves for the control plane rather than for a party. The runner makes them as 'scheduler' and 'system', or as the worker for a cancellation. The governed world's registry (tools/adversarial_eval.py), found by granting each act a refusal named, gives those two parties keys and no grant, because nothing refused them.
findings.reproduction: At c82541e, under a registry granting PROPOSER, EXECUTOR and VERIFIER over stage10.emit_artifact to the runner's three parties: a governed run reaches VERIFIED; 'mallory', named by no grant, moves it to INVALIDATED as SYSTEM, both through GovernedTasks.invalidate and by an appended record; she rejects a CREATED task as SCHEDULER and cancels another as SYSTEM. GovernedTasks.projection() and reconstruct_tasks hold each move, with nothing unauthorized. Her own create is refused, NOT_GRANTED. And on the adversarial evaluation's governed world (tools/adversarial_eval.py), after its legitimate task succeeded: its registered colleague, 'ai-colleague', whom no grant names, signs a task.transition moving the first verified task to INVALIDATED as SYSTEM; the history still authenticates, GovernedTasks.projection() and reconstruct_tasks hold the task INVALIDATED with nothing unauthorized, and verify_in_separate_process answers ok.
findings.observed: Found reading agent_substrate/governed_tasks.py in full, comparing its registry roles with the record authority's.
findings.expected: A move the control plane makes is made by a principal the registry names for it, as the record authority's SYSTEM is.
findings.correction: None in code: which principal the control plane is, and which registry role stands behind its moves, is the owner's to decide. A grant for the runner's 'scheduler' and 'system' would need a role the registry does not have, or VERIFIER and PROPOSER grants that would let either verify or submit. _TASK_REGISTRY_ROLES now states every move the two roles make, and the trust-boundary matrix says no grant stands behind them.
findings.residual_risk: Under a registry any principal that can append a record, and under a governed history any that holds a key, can reject, cancel or time out any task, take its lease or return it to the queue, and withdraw any verified task and with it every result resting on it. None of this forges a verdict: nothing it reaches moves a task or a result to VERIFIED.
